issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Arun is a 44-year-old married nurse who came to treatment months after being mugged on his way home from an evening hospital shift. The assault happened in the hospital parking structure, a place he had always treated as routine and forgettable. He remembers the fluorescent lights, the concrete pillar beside his car, and the sudden movement of a man coming out from between vehicles. What stays with him most are the visual fragments: a hand reaching, the flash of metal, the angle of the attacker's face, the ground rushing up when he was struck. Even now he describes the event as if he is looking at photographs rather than remembering a continuous story, and when those images come back, he feels pain in the same places that were hurt during the robbery. The parking garage at work remains especially potent because it so closely matches the scene of the attack; finishing a shift and walking toward his car can make him feel as if he is stepping back into that same moment.

In the weeks after the mugging, Arun began to make sense of what happened in harsh, personal terms. He had come to believe there was something about him that made the event happen, as if he had looked weak, inattentive, or like an easy target. From there his view of the future narrowed quickly. When he turned these ideas over in his mind, the visual fragments of the mugging became easier to summon and harder to dismiss; the attack sat in front of him like evidence that he really had been exposed and helpless. The more he judged himself as the kind of man this could happen to, the more vividly he found himself back with the flash of metal and the ground rushing up at him. He found himself thinking that nothing good could happen to him anymore and, more bleakly, that he had no future in any meaningful sense. Those conclusions did not stay abstract. Because he was certain the world had become permanently unsafe and that he himself was somehow marked for harm, he started living defensively: checking mirrors repeatedly, keeping his mind occupied whenever possible so he would not have to dwell on what had happened, and constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of threat.

That sense of danger spread into nearly every part of daily life. Arun began choosing seats in staff meetings, the break room, and restaurants based on whether his back was protected and whether he could see exits. Walking through the hospital corridors or crossing the parking lot, he looked behind him again and again to check whether someone was following. Nights became difficult; he struggled to fall asleep and woke easily, alert to minor sounds in the house. The more he felt under threat, the more convinced he became that his life had been permanently damaged. During long wakeful hours he would think that a man who could not even get to his car safely had no real future, and this fear-driven vigilance only tightened his need to monitor every space he entered.

His memory of the robbery did not soften with time. Instead, the continued sense of threat seemed to sharpen it. If he heard footsteps behind him after a shift or noticed his reflection unexpectedly in a glass door, vivid images of the assault would flare up with startling clarity. He would not simply remember being hit; he would feel the pain return in his body as though the attack were happening again. Those moments left him feeling sure that the mugging had changed him fundamentally. The fact that the images arrived so forcefully seemed, to Arun, like proof that he was broken beyond repair and that whatever future he had imagined for himself had already been cut off.

To manage this, he tried harder and harder to stay in control. He kept his mind busy constantly-podcasts during his commute, television left on at home, charting longer than necessary at work-anything to avoid an unoccupied moment. He checked mirrors repeatedly, including reflective surfaces in the unit, to reassure himself no one was approaching unnoticed. He scanned parking areas, hallways, and elevators for danger. Yet these habits seemed to keep the robbery close. Catching his own reflection while checking behind him could suddenly call up a frozen visual image of the attacker; relentless scanning made every movement in the periphery feel significant enough to pull the memory forward. Afterward he would judge himself even more severely, seeing his inability to put the event away as further evidence that there was something fundamentally wrong with him.

The cycle has begun to alter his work and home life in concrete ways. At the hospital he lingers until other staff are leaving so he does not have to walk alone, and when no protected seat is available he becomes distracted, tracking doors and footsteps more than conversations. His wife has noticed that even when they go out to eat, he studies mirrors and keeps choosing seats against the wall, rarely relaxing. Arun sought help only after realizing that his world had become organized around preventing another attack and around escaping the images of the first one, neither of which was working. What frightens him most is the thought that he is already living the rest of his life in that parking garage, with no future beyond vigilance; what he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that he might somehow stop feeling hunted by both the world and his own mind.
